In the months following the crash, the National Transportation Safety Board investigated the cause. The report includes an excerpt from the pilot himself, where he admits to miscalculating variables of weight and fuel consumption. Although he filled his tank prior to the over 1,000-mile flight from Aguadilla, Puerto Rico, one of his two engines failed during descent, possibly due to running out of fuel. The last engine couldn't support the weight and lost altitude, leading to the forced landing just three miles from their destination at North Perry Airport. The NTSB calculated, he exceeded the maximum capacity of the plane by over 625 pounds. North Perry Airport itself has grown its own controversy, as 35 reported crashes have happened in the past five years. North Perry is listed as Florida's largest general aviation airport. They are equipped with 11 flight training schools, despite the large number of residents living around it. There were over 317,000 flights recorded in 2024. equating to one landing or take-off every minute of every day from 7 in the morning to 9 at night. The same hours the air traffic tower is staffed. The airport reportedly projected they wouldn't reach those numbers for another 10 years. Pembroke Pines Mayor Angelo Castillo shared his two cents. You've got people practicing how to take off and land who aren't yet licensed pilots. The miracle is, we haven't had more crashes. As of posting this video, the airport is still in full operation. The pilot is not being criminally charged, and any repercussions he may have faced are not publicly available.
